This paper focuses primarily on how to increase financial flows to adaptation and resilience. Given the focus on increasing finance, it places less emphasis on the equally important and related questions of finance quality, such as what adaptation solutions should be funded, what impact the projects ultimately have, or who should make these funding decisions. Following the structure of the Circle of Ministers Report, it looks at actions that, taken together, could add up to a significant and impactful shift in finance toward climate resilience in developing nations.

This paper employs qualitative, desk-based research drawing on secondary data sources to examine trends, challenges, and opportunities in adaptation finance. It synthesizes existing academic research, policy reports, and data from multilateral organizations to develop a comprehensive understanding of the landscape of adaptation financing.

The analysis proceeds in two steps. First, a systematic literature review was conducted of peer-reviewed articles. Second, the study incorporates grey literature—including reports from intergovernmental organizations (e.g., UNFCCC, Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, World Bank, Green Climate Fund), non-governmental organizations, and think tanks—to capture recent policy developments and financial commitments. These documents were selected based on their credibility, transparency in data collection, and relevance to adaptation finance. This approach aims to provide a comprehensive overview and identifying gaps for future research.

This study analyzes 162 cases of financial instruments for climate adaptation over the past decade to identify patterns that support governments, funders, and financial institutions seeking to scale adaptation finance. The range and increasing num-

Financial instruments for adaptation must respond to a range of context-specific factors, including physical risks, macro-fiscal conditions, institutional capacities, and business environments. The primary limitation of this study is the availability of data on finance for adaptation, which is an evolving and debated concept. While not an exhaustive or statistically representative sample of the current financial landscape for adaptation, the study’s sample is nonetheless illustrative of the diversity of financial instruments available for adaptation and disaster risk management and their uses across a range of risks, geographies, and actors.

In addition, this study’s methodology and subsequent findings face the following limitations:

The 11 financial instrument types included in this study reflect those commonly used at the time of data collection. They do not, however, include instruments for which there is no or limited publicly available information.

The current analysis does not represent the monetary value of finance mobilized in each case, only the frequency of cases by instrument type. It also does not evaluate the quality of finance mobilized, which varies by instrument type and conditions of deployment. These analyses are beyond the scope of this paper, although integral to a borrower’s full understanding of any given adaptation finance option.

The distribution of instruments in the dataset is representative of the universe of instruments based on a systematic search and SFWG partner recommendations. It is not, however, statistically representative of either the global frequency with which each instrument type may have been used for adaptation or the frequency used in any particular location.

Development-oriented loans from multilateral development banks (MDBs) are not typically captured in this dataset, even though some do build resilience in selected project subcomponents. This is because MDB project descriptions focus on development benefits more than on climate adaptation co-benefits and are therefore not picked up by the search algorithm. As a result, the role of MDB-financed concessional loans is underrepresented in the dataset.

The cases included in this study were identified through mixed methods and compiled into a dataset for analysis. Relevant cases were first sourced from country members and institutional knowledge partners to the Group of Twenty (G20) Sustainable Finance Working Group (SFWG), a key stakeholder group for this study. To complement these recommendations, cases were also identified through a systematic literature review that combined risk- and instrument-specific search terms. Only cases launched since 2015 were included in the analysis.

This study aims to support public and private actors in navigating the current adaptation finance landscape. Readers can search the publicly available dataset to find additional data and references for cases of interest. However, the dataset is not statistically representative of all financial instruments for adaptation by either the frequency with which they have been used or the total volume of finance mobilized. For example, concessional loans from multilateral development banks (MDBs) and other donor grants have traditionally dominated adaptation finance but do not appear with a similar frequency in this dataset (see “Methodology”). Nevertheless, the study represents a first effort to connect different types of financial instruments with various physical climate risks, illustrating the growing level of diversity in the adaptation finance landscape.

report.title: Adaptation finance accountability: tracking, transparency and civil society
keyPoints: The Adaptation Finance Accountability Initiative (AFAI) is a collaborative research and advocacy project that works to improve transparency and accountability for adaptation finance. It was launched in 2012 and works with civil society organisations in Nepal, the Philippines, Uganda and Zambia [1][2][3].

The report describes an accountability gap: local accountability for adaptation finance is just getting started, and CSOs in recipient countries need support and advice to monitor and advocate for accountable use of funds [4][2].

Information about adaptation finance is scattered across different levels of donor and recipient governments and databases, and is often difficult to obtain. This hinders community participation in decisions and limits the role of civil society [5][6].

AFAI research finds that projects labelled adaptation do not always address climate risks or contribute to adaptation, which complicates tracking. Data are also not always available to hold finance providers to account [7][8].

AFAI frames accountability around five principles: transparency, ownership, responsiveness, participation and equity. These can be applied from national to local levels and can start a dialogue on the effectiveness of adaptation finance [9].

Tracking adaptation finance is presented as the starting point for a national accountability discussion, giving an evidence base for advocacy and an initial indication of how much committed funding is actually spent on adaptation projects [10][11].

In the Philippines, iCSC used publicly available information to identify many donor-funded projects tagged as adaptation-relevant but not captured by the government. This sparked interest from the House of Representatives, which strengthened oversight of adaptation finance flows [12].

paragraphs: WRI's 2025 Year in Review describes 2025 as a big year for the ocean, anchored by the UN Ocean Conference co-hosted by France and Costa Rica [1]. The Our Ocean Conference progress update, a 2026 working paper, notes that UNOC3 in June 2025 adopted the Nice Ocean Action Plan and produced over 800 new voluntary commitments [2]. The same update reports that the 10th Our Ocean Conference in April 2025 mobilized 285 new commitments valued at more than US$9 billion [3]. Its tally of 2,900 commitments across six action areas shows 1,200 complete, 1,179 in progress and 521 not started [4].

On governance, the BBNJ (High Seas Treaty) reached its 60-country ratification threshold in September 2025 and entered into force in January 2026 [2]. The WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies also entered into force after more than two decades of negotiations, and it prohibits subsidies that contribute to illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing [1]. Not all news was positive: the August 2025 plastics treaty session in Geneva ended with no outcome, deep-sea mining negotiations lacked consensus, and countries voted to postpone adoption of the IMO Net Zero Framework for one year [2].

A separate WRI working paper on 2025 nationally determined contributions analyzed 66 new or updated island and coastal country NDCs received as of November 6, 2025 [5]. It found 53 NDCs with coastal and marine conservation adaptation actions and 39 with climate-resilient fisheries and aquaculture, while none included ocean-based renewable energy adaptation [5]. For mitigation, 12 NDCs included ocean-based renewable energy [6].

sources.passage:
It is overfished, underfunded and overlooked in conversations about food, biodiversity and human health. Its alarm bells are ringing, with record high temperatures, increasingly acidic waters and unfathomable quantities of pollution. Despite these problems and the importance of the ocean in maintaining a healthy, stable planet, it takes a back seat in international environmental conversations, falling far down the list of global priorities.

As we approached the beginning of the year, there appeared to be an opportunity to address the ocean’s challenges head-on. 2025 would bring an unusually high concentration of attention to the problems of our waters. Among these opportunities were a range of deadlines, milestones and new initiatives aimed at transforming ocean governance, conservation and sustainable development. Anchored by the UN Ocean Conference, co-hosted by France and Costa Rica, it was clear that 2025 was a big year for the ocean.

And beyond individual nations offering a roadmap to cleaning up their national waters, we also saw a major milestone in addressing overfishing. In September, the World Trade Organisation (WTO) Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies entered into force when it was ratified by two thirds of the WTO member nations. It took more than two decades of negotiations to reach this agreement, which prohibits subsidies that contribute to illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing.

In 2025, several key international ocean milestones were reached, while others require renewed focus, ambition, and action to become truly effective.

Entry into force of the High Seas Treaty.The Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ) reached the 60-country ratification threshold in September 2025 and entered into force in January 2026. This represents a critical pathway to achieve the global 30x30 goal and protect the high seas.

Entry into force of the World Trade Organization Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies (Fish 1).Following over 20 years of negotiations, this agreement puts in place measures to curb illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing and fishing of overfished stocks, a practice estimated to cost US$22 billion globally per year.a

The third United Nations Ocean Conference (UNOC3).Hosted by the governments of France and Costa Rica in June 2025, UNOC3 resulted in the adoption of the Nice Ocean Action Plan and produced over 800 new voluntary commitments.b

International legally binding agreement on plastic pollution.The fifth negotiation session held in August 2025 in Geneva ended with no outcome, and negotiations are expected to continue. A coordinated global response to plastic pollution is critical to securing the long-term health of the ocean.

Deep-sea mining.International Seabed Authority member states continued negotiations to establish a mining code for deep-sea extraction but were unable to reach a consensus on provisions needed for commercial activities. Support for a moratorium on deepsea mining from some states has grown, but others are showing increased interest in advancing both exploration and exploitation.

International Maritime Organization Net Zero Framework.Despite approval of the first global shipping net zero framework in April 2025, countries voted to postpone adoption for one year, delaying action to limit emissions and adopt greenhouse gas pricing mechanisms.

The ocean sustains billions of people, regulates the climate, and underpins global biodiversity. Yet it is under mounting pressure from climate change, overexploitation of marine and coastal resources, and pollution (IOC-UNESCO 2024). Global, regional, and national ocean governance to address these complex challenges has historically been fragmented. Ocean finance and investment, in particular, remains underresourced and underallocated (Thiele et al. 2025).

The Our Ocean Conference (OOC) was founded in 2014 to help meet this challenge. The conference brings together governments, private sector, civil society, academia, and coastal communities to generate ambitious commitments to sustainably manage, restore, and conserve the ocean. Commitments and investment pledges are mobilized across six OOC action areas: the ocean-climate nexus, marine protected areas (MPAs), marine pollution, sustainable fisheries, the sustainable blue economy, and maritime security.

To assess the effectiveness of this platform in converting pledges into action, the OOC Secretariat delivered a progress stocktake of 2,600 commitments in 2025 (Lee-Emery et al. 2025). Authors found that 81 percent of commitments made between 2014 and 2024 were reported as “complete” or “in progress.” Additionally, 2.4 percent of all MPAs have

been announced through the OOC, equivalent to 8.7 million square kilometers (Figure 1) (Sullivan-Stack et al. 2025).

In April 2025, the 10th Our Ocean Conference (OOC10) mobilized 285 new commitments to ocean action, valued at more than US$9 billion (Table 1). Beyond OOC, 2025 was a critical year for the ocean, culminating in the ratification of several key treaties and raising the profile of ocean diplomacy worldwide (Box 1).

Despite these successes, the fact that 2025 was a big year for the ocean does not mean that all the news was good.

This was a major victory in its own right, but the way we govern the ocean must be as interconnected as the ocean itself. In addition to the High Seas Treaty that governs waters beyond national boundaries, WRI is working with coastal countries to develop plans to sustainably manage 100% of their own national waters – which collectively add up to a third of the ocean. We’ve played a key role in convening nations large and small to build an ocean economy that balances protection and sustainable use.

For one thing, regulations to address plastic pollution remain uncertain. In August, negotiations on the Global Plastics Treaty fell flat, failing to reach a deal.
